Sparsely populated - save for the wildlife who call this rugged coastline home - the Catlins in the southern tip of the South Island offers views of some of New Zealand’s most stunning natural beauty. Your tour begins at 8am from your accommodation as we head south along the Southern Scenic route, through the sea-side village of Brighton before stopping for photos at the mouth of the mighty Taieri River. Continuing on you will go through Waihola and Balclutha before arriving in Owaka, the gateway to the Catlins. Your first short walk takes you to Nugget Point, the most iconic landform of the Otago Coastline. From here you will see the several rugged rocks likened to gold nuggets where NZ fur seals and many NZ seabirds can be viewed. If you visit between December and February there is always the chance of seeing a huge Elephant Seal from the viewing platform. Continuing south our next stop is at a picturesque bay known to be a favourite haul-out site for the rarest sea lion in the world, the New Zealand sea lion. After being hunted to near extinction, only about 200 remain on the mainland. Stand in awe of their magnificence, you’ll be as close as 10 metres from one of these wonderful marine mammals. Driving through native coastal rainforest surrounded by ancient trees your next short walk takes you to the highest waterfall in the Catlins. Your guide will introduce you to several native bush birds and native plants before you arrive at the McLean Falls, arguably the most spectacular of all the waterfalls in the Catlins. Further south you will get the opportunity to look for one of the rarest and smallest dolphins in the world – the Hectors dolphin. The nutrient-rich waters attract this dolphin to become resident in one of the bays on the Catlins coast during the warmer months. Approximately 20 minutes’ drive from Wellington, overlooking the sparkling Pauatahanui Inlet and linked with Battle Hill (a significant Maori War site), Shenandoah is a working farm and hidden historical gem inside a native wild birdlife reserve. Originally a Maori Fortress Pa for Ngati Toa in the 1800’s, the property has seen three different owners over 150 years. Riding a trick skateboard is an exhilarating experience that combines balance, agility, and creativity. Designed specifically for performing tricks, these skateboards feature smaller, harder wheels and narrower decks compared to cruisers or longboards. These characteristics make trick skateboards ideal for technical manoeuvres like ollies, flips, grinds, and aerial tricks, especially in skate parks and urban environments.
The first step in mastering a trick skateboard is building a solid foundation in balance and control. Learning how to properly stand on the deck, control your speed, and steer using your body weight are essential skills. Once comfortable, riders can begin practising basic tricks like the ollie, which is the foundation of many more advanced tricks. An ollie allows skaters to lift the board off the ground without using their hands and is crucial for jumps and aerial stunts.
As riders progress, they can experiment with more advanced tricks like kickflips, where the skateboard rotates underfoot while airborne, or grinding on rails and ledges. Each trick requires precise foot placement and timing, demanding hours of practice to perfect. Skating on smooth surfaces like concrete in skate parks or streets is ideal for these types of tricks, as hard wheels give better speed and control on such surfaces.
In addition to technique, riding a trick skateboard also emphasises creativity and personal style. Skaters often combine tricks, develop their own variations, and find unique spots in urban landscapes to showcase their skills. The individuality of skating is a big part of its appeal, making it more than just a sport, but a form of self-expression.
Overall, riding a trick skateboard requires patience, practice, and persistence, but the rewards are immense. It’s a challenging, dynamic sport that continually pushes your limits, offering an ever-evolving sense of accomplishment and fun.

We'll begin at the Wallagoot Lake Sailing Club and prepare for our night adventure. The sandy dunes along the shore are a great spot to see kangaroos as they come out to graze at dusk.

Using our special underwater light, we'll search for fish, prawns, jellyfish, and even stingrays in the shallow, protected waters below. With lights on each kayak, we'll paddle safely back together, savouring this surreal and serene experience.
